source.title: Exploring the Interchangeability of CNN Embedding Spaces
source.authors: David G. McNeely-White; Benjamin Sattelberg; Nathaniel Blanchard; R. Beveridge

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Numerical cells from Tables 2 and 6 are not included in the supplied text; only the tables’ descriptions and the authors’ prose summaries are available.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether learned CNN embedding spaces can be mapped linearly with little loss, using ridge-regression maps and task accuracy rather than a direct representation-similarity measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports mapped classification and face-verification outcomes, plus explicit statements about the limitations of accuracy as a similarity proxy. Table 2 and Table 6 are described but their individual cells are absent from the supplied text, so no model-by-model table values are extracted. Reported model accuracies and model sizes used as context are not separate mapping outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study fits ridge-regression linear maps between the penultimate embeddings of 10 ImageNet CNNs with different architectures, and of 4 face CNNs differing in architecture and/or training data. It scores each map by the task accuracy it preserves. This directly tests V4 (a simple linear map with little loss) by a method different from the originals. It also reports a qualitative accuracy-related pattern bearing on V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that CNN embeddings trained for a common task are largely interchangeable through empirically estimated linear maps, across architectures and, for faces, different training datasets. They also warn that accuracy under a classifier-derived map can overstate similarity, and note that some information does not transfer. They present this as empirical support for Roeder et al.'s theory that models converge to the same representation up to a linear transform.
record.recipe_differences: Uses ridge-regression linear maps between paired feature vectors and evaluates task accuracy; it does not use the original sources’ representational-similarity procedures. ImageNet maps use corresponding image features; face maps are fitted using matched identity pairs.
record.method_sensitivity: Mapping performance differs across models; the authors state that Model-MM is outperformed by a large margin and that its lower performance may account for weaker mappings to and from its feature space. The paper also shows that identity maps perform near randomly on LFW, unlike fitted maps.

fits_no_version.finding: Analytic proof that, for full-rank linear classifiers, a map computed from the classifier weights reproduces the source network's accuracy exactly, even into a random-feature system. Mapped accuracy therefore does not imply feature similarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task accuracy after a classifier-derived linear map is not a valid measure of representational similarity.

record.problems: The supplied text omits the individual numerical cells of Tables 2 and 6, leaving only aggregate prose summaries for the mapping results. Classification accuracy is an indirect proxy for feature similarity, and the paper itself demonstrates that classifier-based analytic maps can preserve accuracy without establishing similar features. The supplied text does not report uncertainty for the mapped-result summaries.
record.rows_left_out: Individual model-to-model mapping values from Tables 2 and 6 could not be recorded because their cells are absent from the supplied text. No other reported mapping-result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: No controlled scale sweep; no language or other modalities; the models share a dataset and objective (ImageNet), so the 'different data and objectives' part is untested on the classification side.
No vision-language or paired image-caption models.
No stitching, relative representations or unpaired mapping; only final-layer embeddings; only within-task maps.
No interpretable features, neurons or circuits.
No comparison of similarity metrics or input distributions. The paper only raises an analytic caveat about the accuracy proxy.
No plateau test and no test of shared data or objectives as the cause. Transfer losses are small rather than far from complete.

missing.what: Specific cell: ResNet-v2-152's classifier fed linearly mapped PNASNet features reaches 82.46%, versus 78.70% unmapped. The authors add that no feature vector becomes more discriminative relative to its own source network.
Per-pair mapped accuracies for the 10 ImageNet CNNs and the 4 face CNNs (needed to check the accuracy-loss pattern claimed for V1 and the Model-MM weakness).
missing.locator: Tables 2 and 6 (cells not in supplied text)

missing.what: Mapping to the random-weight control gives poor accuracy, which the authors use to argue their empirical maps exploit real feature similarity.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 'challenges' label was wrong: the analytic caveat is about the authors' own proxy, and if anything it is consistent with metric dependence rather than challenging it. It is not an empirical convergence measurement. The record's V7 labels were dropped because the reported transfer losses are small. The V1 evidence is a single qualitative sentence within one dataset and task.

versions.untested_parts: No controlled sweep that scales a model while holding other factors fixed; no language or cross-modal models; the ImageNet models share a dataset and task.
No study of networks trained from different initializations of the same architecture or of shared features/subspaces across seeds.
The study tests empirically fitted linear maps on classification and face-verification tasks. It does not test stitching, relative representations, or mapping without paired training examples.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are identified.
The paper demonstrates a limitation of classification accuracy as a similarity proxy, but does not compare a range of similarity metrics or test out-of-distribution inputs.
The paper reports some incomplete transfer and model-dependent outcomes, but does not test for a plateau or establish shared training data/objectives as the cause of alignment.

rows.subject: 10 ImageNet-trained CNNs (aggregate over pairwise mappings)
rows.operation_detail: Fit empirical linear feature-space maps and measure mapped classification accuracy

conditions.value: validation set, described as unseen during mapping training

rows.measure: Percent change in classification accuracy after mapping, relative to the source CNN
rows.value: The percent change was no worse than -11.6%; the median percent change over mappings was -1.90%.
rows.note: Aggregate prose summary; the individual Table 2 mapping cells are absent from the supplied text. The authors say the results suggest that features learned by one CNN are also learned by the others, while some models have superior variations.
rows.check: Aggregate over pairwise maps (worst -11.6%, median -1.90%) shows near-lossless mapping. It is not a scale trend, so it does not bear on V1. Loss this small is not 'far from complete' alignment, so it does not bear on V7.

rows.subject: 10 ImageNet-trained CNNs (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compare classification-accuracy changes across mapped CNN combinations

conditions.value: source CNN accuracy and mapped accuracy

rows.measure: How accuracy loss after mapping varies with source-network accuracy
rows.value: The sharpest accuracy dropoffs occur for the lowest-accuracy networks.
rows.note: The authors interpret this pattern as suggesting that sufficiently complex architectures converge to similar solutions. The supplied text does not give the individual values supporting this comparison.
rows.check: Qualitative only: authors say the sharpest mapping losses occur for the lowest-accuracy networks. No per-network values are in the supplied text. Weak evidence: the pattern could also reflect less expressive source features rather than greater convergence. Within one dataset and task.

rows.subject: Four face-recognition CNNs (aggregate over directed mappings)
rows.operation_detail: Fit empirical linear maps between embeddings and evaluate face verification

conditions.value: 2,700 matched image pairs per mapping fold

rows.value: The loss in accuracy introduced by linear mapping is at most 1.0% on LFW.
rows.note: Aggregate result; individual Table 6 cells are absent from the supplied text. The authors also say that some information does not transfer, while the vast majority is equivalent.
rows.check: At most 1.0% LFW accuracy loss across 12 directed maps, including maps between the same architecture trained on different datasets. Does not bear on V7.

rows.subject: Four face-recognition CNNs (aggregate identity-map comparisons)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate face verification using an identity map instead of a fitted inter-model map
rows.note: The authors use this comparison to distinguish fitted mappings from direct interchangeability of the original feature coordinates.
rows.check: Identity-map control (near-random accuracy). It shows the coordinates are not directly shared; it is not a test of whether a fitted simple map works. No baseline value is given.

rows.subject: Randomly initialized PNASNet-Large
rows.operation_detail: Map random-network features to trained CNN classifiers and measure classification accuracy
rows.value: Improved by as much as two orders of magnitude, but reached only about 5% in the best case.
rows.note: The paper presents this as a control and notes that the architecture may encode useful information independently of learned weights.
rows.check: Random-weight PNASNet control (about 5% best case). It is a control for the method, not a measurement of convergence between trained models.

rows.subject: Linear-classifier CNNs (analytic mapping result)
rows.operation_detail: Derive a classifier-based analytic linear map from the two classifiers
rows.value: The analytic map can give accuracy exactly equal to the source system's accuracy, even though the authors show that this does not establish feature-space similarity; they give random features as an example.
rows.note: The paper explicitly warns that high mapped accuracy is not sufficient evidence of high feature-space similarity. This is an analytic result and illustrative example, not a separate empirical mapping-table result.
rows.check: Analytic theorem that a classifier-derived map can preserve accuracy even with dissimilar features. It is a methodological caveat about the accuracy proxy, not an empirical measurement of convergence. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Face-recognition CNNs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Assess information transfer under fitted linear mappings between face embeddings
rows.value: The authors state that some information does not transfer, although the vast majority of information encoded by each network is equivalent.
rows.note: Qualitative summary; it does not quantify the amount of information that fails to transfer.
rows.check: The authors state that some information does not transfer, but the vast majority is equivalent. Unquantified. It qualifies V4 slightly; it does not show the incomplete or plateauing alignment V7 describes.

relationships.condition: Linear ridge maps between penultimate embeddings of ImageNet CNNs and of face CNNs (different architectures and/or training sets)
relationships.reason: Median ImageNet mapped-accuracy change was -1.90% (worst -11.6%), and LFW loss was at most 1.0% (r1, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Mapped ImageNet accuracy changed by −1.90% at the median and −11.6% in the worst case, while LFW loss stayed at or below 1.0%.

relationships.condition: Face-embedding maps, especially those involving the weaker Model-MM
relationships.reason: The authors say some information does not transfer, and maps to and from Model-MM perform worse; the losses are unquantified in the rows (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Some information failed to transfer between face embeddings, with mappings to and from Model-MM performing worse.

relationships.condition: ImageNet-trained CNNs of varying accuracy, same data and task
relationships.reason: The authors report the largest mapping losses for the lowest-accuracy networks, read as convergence with capability. Qualitative only, without per-network numbers (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Mapping losses were largest for the lowest-accuracy networks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Mapped accuracy changes were generally small, and the authors report sharper losses for lower-accuracy networks as a pattern consistent with greater convergence at higher capability (r1, r2).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Empirically fitted mappings on ImageNet classification and LFW face verification
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that fitted linear maps largely preserved classification and face-verification accuracy (r1, r3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Direct identity mapping and incomplete face-embedding transfer
reader_labels.reason: Original face-embedding coordinates gave near-random accuracy without a fitted map, and the authors report that some information did not transfer (r4, r7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Transfer was not complete, although the authors characterize the untransferred information as a small part of what the networks encode (r3, r7).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Classifier-based analytic mapping evaluated by classification accuracy
reader_labels.reason: The analytic construction can preserve source accuracy without establishing similar feature spaces, so this accuracy measure can overstate representation similarity (r6).
